utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we please have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Matthias Neuner, for the Prosecution assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues from the Prosecutor's office, to everyone in and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, with Mr. Nicholas Robson, representing General Rasim Delic, with our legal assistant, Lejla Gluhic, and our intern, Ms. Tineke Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I believe the parties have something to raise before we call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure if the Defence does, but certainly the Prosecution has two very quick issues to raise. The first issue concerns a motion filed on the 10th of March, 2008, for protective measures. The Prosecution will take no position with respect to that application. It's clearly a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide if protective measures are merited, and we will not be filing a written response. And therefore, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, that matter is ready for the Trial Chamber to determine. Secondly, also on the 10th of March, 2008, the Defence filed a motion for the adjournment of the hearing on the 1st and 2nd of April. As was the case with the motion for protective measures, the Prosecution takes no position with respect to the Defence request. Certainly, that's a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide, and we neither oppose nor support that motion. I do note, however, that there is a reference in that motion to a witness whose apparently scheduled to appear on the 3rd and 4th of April, 2008. To this, as of today, we have not received any information concerning the schedule for the month of April, in terms of Defence witnesses, and I would again ask that to the extent possible, we be provided with as much advance notice of the anticipated dates that the Defence intends to call their witnesses as possible. Clearly, in this application, there is reference to a witness being scheduled to appear, but that was actually the first we'd heard of that witness and the proposed dates for his appearance, so I simply want to put that on the record. But with respect to the issue of whether an adjournment is merited for the reasons stated in the motion, that is clearly up to the Trial Chamber to decide, and we will not take a position on that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis, and thanks for the position that the Prosecution takes on the point. I would imagine that the Defence did hear, insofar as the next witness for April is concerned that is mentioned in the second motion, and that as soon as is possible for them to do so, they will make sure that you're provided with the necessary information. Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would like to call Mr. Halim Husic as our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought into the court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you know, I'm Vasvija Vidovic, and I will be putting questions to you today on behalf of General Delic's Defence. What I would like to draw your attention to is the following: We speak the same language, and it's very important that my question and your answer be recorded in the transcript and that we do not overlap when speaking. So I kindly ask you that after I finish my question, you leave some time for the interpreters to translate the question and then to begin your answer. Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, when and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of September, 1958, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And which schools did you complete after --

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: After elementary school, I completed the high school, the Medresa in Sarajevo, and then I graduated from the Faculty of Theology, Islamic Sciences, also at the Faculty of Theology in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Remember to pause after the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, can you tell us what is your profession now?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a professor at the Gazi Husref Medresa in Sarajevo. I teach history.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, do you speak Arabic?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what duties were you carrying out during the war, if any?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: During the war, from May 1992 until November 1992, I was a member of the Han Bila Detachment, attached to the Travnik Municipality Territorial Defence. After that, from November 1992 until December 1993, I was a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade. I was a assistant commander for morale in that brigade. After that, for three months, I was at the Supreme Command Staff at the forward command post in Kakanj at the organ for morale, and after that, from February 1993 -- sorry, 1994, I was in the 3rd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was first deputy commander for morale and then, as of April 1995, I was the assistant commander for morale in the 3rd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina until I was demobilized from the army after 1545 days which I spent in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the number of days? It's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: 1545 days I was a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 1545 days, this is what you said?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you testify before this Tribunal before?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I testified in the Kubura-Hadzihasanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And will you please tell us where you happened to be when the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in February 1992, to be more precise, I went to the Republic of Croatia officially on business, and I spent a month in Umag in Istria. After that, I came to Zagreb, intending to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I understood, from the particulars that you provided, that at the time you were a religious official, you had -- you were a member of the clergy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were in Zagreb, do you recall if there was a mosque there?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a mosque, and I was actually staying on premises that were right next to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So to be quite clear about the time period, we're talking about the spring of 1993 -- no, 1992. I apologise. Did you notice if anything was happening in the mosque or around the mosque at that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At the time, the mosque in Zagreb, and Zagreb in generally was the destination of a large number of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina who were arriving daily, because of the combat actions being conducted in northern parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the one hand, and on the other hand, a vast number of workers were arriving from Western European countries who wanted to link up with their families, provide them with assistance or find out some more information about actually what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was actually a very chaotic state at the time, because a large number of families were separated. They didn't know what was happening with the rest of their family. They didn't know where to go. They didn't have any basic funds to live. They didn't have personal documents. Generally, it was chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, thank you very much for your detailed answer, but I would like to focus now on something else. The mosque in Zagreb and around it, did you notice any people who were not originally from Europe?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, there was a large number of Arabs coming to the mosque every day. They were together with my colleagues or some of my students that I had taught and who at the time were studying in Arab countries, Jordan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you, personally, did you have any contacts with any of those foreigners?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in contact with a large number of them, because all of us actually had a common problem, and that was the inability to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is what we wanted to do. We tried to get some documents or get information about how we could enter Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about how the Arabs were finding their way in Croatia, the ones that you had contacts with?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Compared to us and a large number of Bosniaks refugees who didn't have any documents with them, so their movements were limited, the police in town checked IDs, so our movements were limited. But a considerable number of those people already had Croatian documents, passports, personal ID cards. They had considerable sums of money. They were moving around freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, excuse me for interrupting. Mrs. Vidovic, could we just establish the time? Is it still spring of 1992 that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say, "But a considerable number of those people already had Croatian documents, passports, personal IDs," which people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people of Arab origin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you about, Mr. Husic, is this: Were you able to observe that these Arabs had contacts with other people in Croatia or not? Did you pay any attention to that?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to they're being able to move around freely, a number of them spent some time every day with uniformed men, members of the Croatian Army, but also with some Bosniak units which at the time had their headquarters in Zagreb. And from there, they went to Northern Bosnia, to the battlefields. I know the names of some of those commanders, such as the unit of the Commander Ermin Pohrana, Ekrem Mandal, my neighbor, Midhat Puric, a.k.a. Hadzija, and some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify this a little bit, you said that there were members of the Croatian Army who moved around, but also members of Bosniak units that were seated in Zagreb, so let's clarify that, please, for the record. Were these men, the Bosniaks, members of the Croatian Army or of some other armed force at the time?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian Army which, as independent units, went to various battlefields in Posavina from Zagreb. I know from Midhat Puric, specifically, that he went almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, have I understood you correctly, Midhat Puric was a member of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please see Exhibit 1127. This is a video clip, so in fact it's video 1127.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please stop it here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please look at this frame that you can see on the screen. Can you recognise anyone in this frame?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This person with a beard and the blue cap on the head, in the central position on this video clip, is Midhat Puric, a.k.a. Hadzija.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, Madam Vidovic, your witness's testify will have more probative value if you ask him to ask the video to stop when you have put the question, not for you to stop and then ask a question. Put the question and ask him to stop the video when he gets to that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will certainly do that in the future. I tried to establish whether one person could be recognized there, but he was -- he appeared with his back turned, and I didn't want the witness to comment on that. But I would now like to go back to this individual, Midhat Puric, that you saw in the frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, Witness, is this the person or not that you mentioned earlier as a member of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us a bit more about this person, please? Did he come to Bosnia-Herzegovina at some point in time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in Zagreb, myself, he called me up. He asked me to come to his unit, and he told me that he would soon go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a man that I knew from childhood. We were neighbours. At first I agreed, because this was the only way that I could actually enter Bosnia-Herzegovina, but when I told Mr. Semso Pankovic about this, who knew about my stay in Zagreb, he advised that I should not join such units, and that if I wanted to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina as an individual, I should go as an individual and then join the armed forces. However, when I arrived, and this trip took over a month, in our area, in our native town, Mehurici, I found Mr. Puric and his unit there, and this unit was very well armed. I don't know exactly how many men it numbered; 20 to 30, I think. And we often referred to them as "Zengas" because earlier on they had fought in Croatia. And on their part, at this time they joined the Patriotic League, because Midhat's close relative was at the head of the Patriotic League in Zenica. I cannot recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. Now I would like to show you a document. Could the witness please be shown D801. This is a document from the Ministry of Defence of Republic of Croatia, SIS, of the 19th of September, 1992. Could the witness please be shown page 2 of the document right away: The English version, 2, page 2 also. Thank you. Are you able to read this document, Mr. Husic?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the copy is pretty bad. The English version is clearer, but the Bosnian version is very difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give the witness a hard copy of this document. Also, if possible, could you please just zoom in on the first three paragraphs of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please read the text on this page from the beginning up to about half page.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: "Information on the arrival of the Mujahedin ... "

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, would you please just read it to yourself. And then once you've read it, could you please just comment on what it's about. Just please take your time to read it. Okay, now we have the document in English as well. Could you now please give us the answer?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I was just talking about. So a large number of Arabs, as we called them at the time, used to go with these armed groups in Posavina and join the fighters there, in other words, the Croatian units, units of the Croatian Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence. But before that, can we just make this perfectly clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that these were Croatian units or HVO units?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, because of the heading, for one, and also because this information comes from the Ministry of Defence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information to this effect while you were in Croatia and when you wanted to go back to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already mentioned this. I saw these people going daily and coming back, and socializing with these uniformed men from the Croatian Army or from independent units which also belonged to the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, may we have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit 1199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago during your testimony, you mentioned that you managed to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that this took a while, that this was a long journey. How much time did you spend on this trip, on this journey, and could you also tell us, just by way of comparison, normally how long does this trip last?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: My attempt to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina, this trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina took over a month. Normally, this would take just a couple of hours or, at most, half a day, or a full day if you were to take some public transportation bus. However, at this time no roads leading to Bosnia and Herzegovina were under the control of the legal authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that you had to go through a dozen of check-points which you could not get through with personal documents alone on you. It was necessary to have a pass issued by the Croatian Army or the HVO, so that I had to travel from Zagreb to Rijeka, Split, along the so-called Put Spasa or road from salvation, after I obtained a certificate from Caritas, I did this through some personal acquaintances, and also I had to pay, and I travelled with a convoy of humanitarian aid and managed in this way to reach Kiseljak, in the vicinity of Sarajevo, with a lot of difficulties along the way. And then I stayed in Kiseljak for 10 days, following which I paid a man, a Croat, to take me in his own vehicle, going on dirt roads to Travnik and to the house of my parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this: Did you have any impressions about why these Mujahedin found it much easier to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina than you did, although you were a religious official?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just an objection to the way the question was phrased. The witness so far has not said that it was easier for the Mujahedin to go to Bosnia, and this is being suggested in this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. What the witness said, if I remember well, he said they moved freely in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may explain. The witness also explained that they were able to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina - perhaps this was something that escaped you - that they were able to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina with the units of the Croatian Army and go to Posavina. Maybe you're not very familiar with Bosnia and Herzegovina, but this is a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when the witness referred to them entering Posavina. But to clarify this, I can rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't rephrase, because now you've told us a lot of information, Madam Vidovic. Can I just refer us, on the transcript, to where the witness said things that you say he just said, just so that your opposite number is satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 12, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, for those of us who don't know the geography, this doesn't mean much. They went, a large number of them, used to go with these armed groups in Posavina and join the fighters there. It doesn't -- yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I also wish to say or note that the witness didn't say this was an easy way to enter Bosnia. And as far as I understood the witness's testimony, he was not taking the route via Posavina, but rather towards the Dalmatija, meaning the south of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that a person who doesn't know what Posavina is would find this part of the question unclear, but I will clarify this with the witness. I agree with my learned friend, that this can cause confusion, so I will proceed step by step. I just wanted to make better use of the time. So, Your Honours, if you permit me, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may continue, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you mentioned Posavina, can you please tell us if Posavina is a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Posavina is the northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina along the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we can move to this next part of the question. When you came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you talk to any of those Arabs about how they entered Bosnia and Herzegovina and if they -- and if you did, what did they say?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. As far as I know, the witness has not stated that upon his arrival in Bosnia, he talked to Arabs, and it's again being suggested here in the question, or the way the question is phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to tell you the truth, I didn't quite understand. From the -- I didn't understand from the objection. From the particulars given by the witness, it is very clear that he came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and now I'm asking him if he spoke with any of the Arabs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that is the gist of the objection. You see, you said in your question: "When you came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you talk to any of the Arabs about how they entered Bosnia and Herzegovina and if they -- and if you did, what did they say?" That was the reason for the objection, that you are suggesting to him that he did talk to them and that they talked to him about the way he entered Bosnia and Herzegovina. You see, I'm just explaining to you what Mr. Neuner's objection was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't believe that this is a leading question. I am simply trying to explore to see if the witness spoke with any of the Arabs about how they entered Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is what is being objected to, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I am going to approach this topic in a different way. I understand your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no position. It's the Prosecution's position. I'm merely explaining it to you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I replied that I did not find this to be a leading question, but that I'm trying to explore if the witness spoke with Arabs or not. But very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Vidovic, I apologise, but if you'd asked the question like you're putting it now, I would have understood, but you asked, "Did you talk to the Arabs about the way they managed to enter, but first you should have asked, "Did you have the opportunity to talk with the Arabs?" That's the problem. Maybe he didn't talk to these Arabs. You don't know right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. As I said, I have a lot of questions, and I'm trying to go faster. But from this point on, this is the way I will be putting my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will go faster, Madam Vidovic, if I may just help, if you ask the questions correctly and evoke no objections. If you have objections, then we're taking more time. Rather than trying to bite too big a bite at a time, take it step by step and you'll go faster. One question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, at some point did you return to Bosnia and Herzegovina or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early May, I returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have the opportunity to speak with any Arabs?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As my parents' house, where I returned at that time and where my family lived, my wife and two under-age children, happened to be near Mehurici. I was surprised because they arrived before I did, and I spoke with one of those with whom I most frequently met in Zagreb because, among other things, he was the one who spoke the Bosnian language the best among them. I think his name was Abdullah. So I asked him how they arrived, did they have any problems on the journey like I did, to which he replied that they had proper documents and that they didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask a question. If you had accepted Mr. Puric's proposal, if you'd agreed to go with him and to cross Posavina, if I remember correctly, do you think it would have been easier for you to reach Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know all the details, how they entered. All I know is that they entered with their own vehicles that they had in Zagreb, with their complete weaponry that they had in Zagreb, and they entered as an organised group, as a military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned documents. Did you talk about what kind of documents those were, these proper documents?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I mentioned at the beginning that the only way to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina was through the HVO territory, but it was not possible to enter via HVO territory without papers from the Croatian state, and that is why I also obtained a document from Caritas in order to be able to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just explain what Caritas is, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Caritas is a humanitarian organisation, but we obtained documents via certain mediators, and they treated us as humanitarian workers on the basis of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you something else, please. What was the relationship of the Croatian and Muslim population in Central Bosnia before the war? This is where you lived; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was born there, completed my elementary school there, and lived there until high school. In places where the Croat and Muslim population was mixed, we went to school together, socialized, worked together, and our relations, especially during the last decade or on the eve of the war, were excellent. From World War II onwards, when this area was actually part of the independent State of Croatia, the relations kept on improving.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You told us that you came in May, if I understood you correctly, to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and where did you come?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I came to the house of my parents in the place of Han Bila, in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Can you briefly describe what was the situation as you found it, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The Bila Valley was in chaos at that point in time. The municipalities from Northwestern Bosnia where places from where a vast number of refugees were arriving daily. Families were separated. They had gone through much suffering. Many didn't know about what happened to other members of their family. They were without any funds, and they were looking for a place to stay, for some sort of refuge.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you came, did you notice if there was any military organisation in that area?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brother and I also immediately joined the Han Bila Detachment, which was part of the TO Staff of the Travnik Municipality, which wasn't actually functioning in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Because the HDZ cadres were blocking its work, and the Croatian people were creating the HOS, the Croat Armed Forces, at the same time, and the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, because of which the Bosniaks started to create mono-ethnic village units which had different names and which were outside of the system of the only legal army, the Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So I'm going to ask you this: Did the Muslim population at that time have a unified military organisation or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know people who -- well, you said that they did not have a unified organisation, and you said that the units had different names. What are those names?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: We were already talking about this group that was called the Patriotic League. Then there were the village units, which were called MOS. Some were calling themselves the Muslim forces, Muslimanske Snage. There was some armed groups taking names, which I don't remember right now, well-sounding names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any point, did you find out anything more about the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was a member of the TO forces and I was interested in why the equipping and arming of those units were proceeding slowly, I came to see some friends and acquaintances, and they invited me to join the MOS, Muslim Armed Forces, because they were being equipped much faster. They tried to convince me that the TO Staff could never function because the Croats were making their own army and obstructing the establishment of a joint army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever join those Muslim forces at any point or not?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. I was opposed to the idea of making a mono-ethnic army because it was contributing to the aggressor's objectives and plans. What particularly bothered me at the time was the fact that these were very young people. Many of them weren't even of age. There was a significant number of my students among them, and I believed that they would suffer very quickly because of that, and this is why this idea was unacceptable to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, now I would like to ask you this: How did your father look at the TO? How did he view the TO?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The TO or the joint army, which was the term that we used more often, as far as the elderly people were concerned and a large number of the Bila Valley population was concerned, too, was, as they said, a partisan army, and it brought them associations to the army from World War II which, during the period of communist rule, considerably narrowed democracy, freedoms and rights in many segments of life, especially in the religious sphere.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already explained to us that you did join the Territorial Defence in Travnik. I will return to this question later, but before that I would like to ask some questions about these foreigners, these Arabs, that we spoke about a little earlier. You mentioned that you contacted a certain -- had contacts with a certain Abdullah. Did you have any other contacts with the Arabs after this?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. A relative of mine, Muradif Husic, was the principal of the elementary school in Mehurici and a member of the Civilian Protection Unit. And as a member of the Civilian Protection, he was ordered to provide accommodation for these Arabs in -- on the premises of the school in Mehurici. After he did this, they began to destroy the facilities of the school, the books, the musical instruments that the school had, and he was unable to communicate with them because he could not speak Arabic. So he asked me to help him to resolve this and to prevent them from vandalizing the school. However, our attempt bore no results whatsoever. They simply ignored us, and the book shelves, they would just topple them over and remove the books and take them to Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "to Rijeka," do you mean Rijeka the city or are you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, I mean the river, the Bila River, which flows through Mehurici. So, in other words, they threw these books into the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me ask you this: Did you discuss with Mr. Muradif Husic who it was who ordered him to provide accommodation for these Arabs on the premises of the school?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him, "What have you brought on to yourself?" And he said that the civilian authorities of the Travnik Municipality ordered the Civilian Defence, or Civilian Protection, to use the school -- to allow the school to be used by this group, which brought in humanitarian aid, because it was in the interests of the refugees and the local population to -- it was in their interests to obtain some food.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, were you able to learn more about what these Arabs did, these Arabs that you saw in the school in Mehurici later on?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the initial activities in providing humanitarian aid, this group began to set up schools, because our schools had stopped -- had closed. And since both my wife and I have a background in theology, one of them, who was in charge of organizing these schools, came to our home and offered -- offered us to teach in these schools. At first, I agreed on the condition that we could use the books and follow the curriculum, as had been followed for decades in Bosnia and Herzegovina in schools, but they refused that and they demanded that we follow their own curricula and use the books that they were very busy and active in printing and distributing all over various towns and places.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this point, I would request that the witness be shown document D1064. Your Honour, this document, let me just say that we have in the e-court system the original Arabic version and the English translation, but we have a copy of the Bosnian version, translation into Bosnian, which we can give to the witness and also to the Prosecutor, in view of the fact that they have an assistant who can speak Bosnian so they can be able to verify this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought I also heard that the witness can understand Arabic. So he can read from the Arabic and tell us what he sees.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we please zoom on this Arabic text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text -- it's a bit difficult to follow this, but basically we can. So this is a call to Jihad and to Allah -- to Allah, the Merciful, and may he be saved as God's prophet, Jihad in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2 of the English version, page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe if you look at the second page, also in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to get the documents to share the screen equally so that we can have the full view of the English version. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to read this from Arabic?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Well, in part, but it's not complete, it's not completely legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you then -- could you please take a look at the Bosnian version. Do you have it in front of you? And I would request that you read the first paragraph on the second page: Witness, do you have the Bosnian version in front of you, not on the screen but in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, in hard copy, not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at page 04685628.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read the first paragraph of this document, the first section of this document, just read it to yourself. Thank you. I will quote the gist of what the Defence would like to point to. At the very beginning of page 2, it says: "Another characteristic of this Jihad is a focus and great care on the missionary aspect, given all elementary and advanced Sharia courses for Ensari [phoen] and Bosnians, equal and serious efforts to establish a complete library in the Bosnian language." I would like to ask you this: You just mentioned that you had opportunity to speak to the Arabs in the Mehurici school about the establishment of their schools, and in relation to that, could you please comment on this portion that you've just read?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This precisely reflects the goals that they had, which completely put aside our tradition in Islamic education in Bosnia, in the Bosnian way of many generations, and they tried to impose a completely new, different concept which had not existed in our parts of the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we please have a number assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit 1200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And would that be a convenient moment, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I was just going to suggest that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, before the break we discussed the religious training or the religious schools organised by Arabs. Did you notice, in the course of 1992 and 1993, any other activities carried out by Arabs?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. After having developed this particular activity and having opened a number of schools, they started calling upon young men, some of them were even under age, to attend a sort of training. In doing so, they equipped them with uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this time, could we look at Exhibit Number 89. And can I kindly ask the usher to zoom in on both documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, while we're waiting for the document to be enlarged, I'll ask you to direct your attention to the second paragraph, starting with the words: "At the command of the 306th ... " Since I'm interested in only a small portion of the document that I want you to comment on, I will quote that, that's the second paragraph of the document. Before dealing with that portion of the document, I want to ask you the following: Can you see what the document deals with, from the heading?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the report on the inspection of the 306th Mountain Brigade that was conducted by the superior command of the 3rd Corps on the 7th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that the date is the 2nd of June, 1993. In connection with this, tell me, were you a member of the brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. The printed number is not very clear. The date, in fact, is that of the 2nd of August, 1993, whereas I had the impression that the date was the 2nd of June, and I misled the witness. Let me quote the relevant part of the document to you. It reads: "At the 306th Mountain Brigade Command in Krpeljici village, the commander of the 4th Battalion of the 306th Brigade, Lujanovic [phoen] informed the brigade chief and us that one platoon from Kotor Varos no longer wished to be part of the 306th Brigade and wished instead to join the 17th Krajina Brigade. A communication was also sent to all the villages from the Muslim forces stationed in Mehurici village, calling soldiers to attend a 40-day training. The question of a timely rotation of personnel in the Ljuta Greda ..." and so on and so forth is being asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you familiar with this problem?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We held the Defence lines at Vlasic, facing the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, my apologies, but could you please focus on the issue of these invitations sent out by the Muslim forces, rather than this other issue of the shortage of men?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The fact is that the young men were being invited to attend training. In view of the conduct of our members, who were onlookers of that process, who were on the flanks holding defence lines, instead of the domestic army, to be in charge of that, they sought that they -- they asked that they join the 17th Glorious Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Evidently, you didn't quite understand what I asked you. I'm interested in the problem, and I'll repeat it again. I'll read: The Muslim forces stationed at Mehuric sent out an invitation to all the villages, inviting young men to attend a 40-day training?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This invitation was sent by the group that we referred to as the Muslim forces, who were in no way an official unit. They were together with the Arabs in part of this training of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim forces are being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Are we talking here of three forces, the 306th -- 4th Battalion, 4th Battalion of the 306th Brigade, the 17th Glorious Krajina Brigade and the Muslim forces? Do I understand it that way, Madam Vidovic, and the Muslim forces, are these what you call the Muslimanske Snage? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will ask the witness to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you referred to the Muslim forces in such documents, what did you have in mind? Was it the MOS or what does "the Muslim forces" stand for, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This isn't the MOS, that particular MOS unit that was being formed in Travnik and that we discussed. This refers to local young men that -- a group of Arabs organised into units by dint of holding training for them, providing them with uniforms, and, in part, weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the relationship, if any, between the local Muslim population and the Arabs in the area of the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population expected that the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina would be stopped by the International Community and the European countries, and these expectations of theirs were not met. The aggression gained momentum, and the only party who provided assistance, primarily large supplies of food and other necessities, were precisely these Arabs. For that reason, the population looked upon their activities favorably and accepted them. They wielded an enormous influence on the population in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You described having had contact with a group of Arabs from Mehurici. Based on what you saw and observed, was that the only group of Arabs, the one that you saw?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. In that period of time, there were several different groups that were oftentimes mutually conflicting and were stationed and active in different areas. Some of them came to the Bila Valley periodically, only to disappear after that, and many of them were stationed in the different parts of the Bila Valley. It was difficult to identify all of them. I know that one of the groups was situated at Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you stop there. When you say one group was situated at Guca Gora, can you tell me what the basis of your knowledge of that is? Did you have any contacts through correspondence?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when the Croatian population left Guca Gora, in addition to the civilian authorities taking care for the abandoned properties --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, please pause there. Can you please specify the time frame? Which period of time are you referring to when you say that the Croatian population left Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: That was the 10th -- the 9th or the 10th of June, 1993. The military police provided security for the monastery at Guca Gora and sent word to the Command of the 306th of the fact that some properties were being set on fire. At that point, the military police or, rather, the Security Service tried to investigate these events, and the young men who were charged with guarding these houses informed the police that the perpetrators were a group called "Abu Hamza." That's how they referred them. That group inhabited the village. They moved into the village at their own will.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with any of the Arab groups in that area at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of June, after the Croatian propaganda had informed the public that the monastery at Guca Gora had been completely damaged and destroyed, the superior command ordered us to send a denial of that piece of news, since it was broadcast by the CNN as well. Thus, I and a group of journalists who had arrived from Zenica set out from Krpeljici to Guca Gora and observed large quantities of household appliances, refrigerators, stoves, and such like, having been taken out of Croat properties by some very strangely-dressed, uniformed persons who had pirate-like scarves on their heads. I walked away from a group of journalists and cameramen with an intention to check who the individuals were. As I walked some 10 metres down toward them, I inquired who they were and which unit they belonged to. I observed that they didn't have any insignia. One of them answered my question rudely by saying, "What do you care about which unit we belong to?" By saying that, he grabbed me by my hair and placed a knife against my neck. A cameraman, who had a camera on him, was trying to film what was going on and adjusting the camera accordingly. When the man holding the knife against my neck noticed that the cameraman was trying to film him, he let go of me and ran toward the cameraman. At that point, there was general commotion already, and the police officers who were providing security for the monastery heard these shouts and headed in our direction. At that point, these individuals fled. They jumped a wall and went away, running among the houses there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, did you ever learn who the individual belonged to, to which group, if any?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I informed the commander of the brigade, and then he informed the superior officer, the commander of the Operations Group Bosanska Krajina, Mr. Alagic, who immediately sent the most elite military police unit that we had to block that entire area and to investigate the entire matter. Our policemen, who were securing the monastery, had already established that these were members of the Gerila from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. When you say "Gerila from Zenica," are these foreigners or locals?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Turkish guerrilla comprising mostly foreigners. I don't know exactly who made up the group, but they are most often referred to in Central Bosnia under this name, "Gerila," a group of foreigners that we could not really ever properly identify. So the trucks that they sent for these looted articles, these were refrigerator trucks of these Zmajevac, butcher's plant from Zenica. They were found completely empty, because in cooperation with some members of the local population, when they understood -- when they realized that there was a search on -- after them, they probably sold or hid the looted articles, so that no one was arrested and the only evidence were the trucks that the military or military police actually seized then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Husic, I would like to ask you this: How far is Guca Gora from the village of Bikosi? I'm referring to the distance.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It's at a distance of some two kilometres away. Bikosi, Maline and Guca Gora are linked by an asphalt road. More recently, those settlements had grown all the way up to the road, so that now you could say that they're almost one populated area, one settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. You described your meetings with Mujahedin in the period of 1992 and early 1993. I would like you to look at some documents, and I would ask you to comment on them, please. Can the witness now look at Exhibit 135, please. For the transcript, this is a daily report of the 3rd Corps Command of the 10th of May, 1993. Witness, can you please look at page 1 in the Bosnian version, and this is page 2 in the English version, Your Honours. Can we scroll down the document in both the Bosnian and the English versions so that we see the lower part of the document. Thank you. Witness, can you please look at this portion. Would you agree that this is referring to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to quote now -- well, please look at this portion, and then after that we will move to the second page of the document. Can we now look at the second page of the Bosnian version of the document. Thank you. Do you see here that there is a portion of the document that is underlined, Mr. Husic?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to that. It says: "We have a lot of problems about the undefined status of the Muslimanske Snage from Mehurici, which according to our information are currently working on the forming of the 8th Muslim Brigade, and there are every day fighters from our brigade who are joining them or reporting to them or to other units." Are you familiar with this situation that is being described in the document?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The forming of the 8th Muslim Brigade is being referred to. According to what you know, was it ever formed?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The 8th Muslim Brigade was never formed. These were just pieces of mis-information spread by these groups in order to attract the largest possible number of individuals from our valley. Our problem was that a large number of our fighters from the 306th, because we still didn't have uniforms or weapons or many other things, reported precisely to these groups, and we needed to stop this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can put this document away. Can the witness now look at Exhibit 88. For the transcript, while we're waiting for the document to appear on the monitor, I can say that this is a document of the 306th Brigade Command, the Section for Morale, dated the 30th of July, 1993, and it talks about the information of the status of combat morale in the area of responsibility and units of the 306th Brigade. This is page 1 of this document. I would like the witness also to look at page 2 of the Bosnian version of this document, which is actually the fourth page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It appears, Mr. Husic, that your name is next to the stamp in the lower right-hand corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I drafted this document as the assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please speak up a little bit? I'm afraid that they don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the commander's person for morale, I was responsible and reporting about the situation of the morale in the situation of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now go back to page 1 of the document, please, the first page of the document. And when it appears in the Bosnian version, I would like to ask you, first of all -- actually, I would like to ask the usher to scroll the Bosnian version of the document down. Also, can we look at page 2 of the English version. We're going to focus on this part that deals with the situation in the units. Can you please show the last two paragraphs of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you look at the last two paragraphs of the document. In English version that would be the last paragraph and then it crosses on to the next page, page 3. So when Their Honours read it, and the Prosecutors reads it, maybe the usher then can show us the next page of the English version. Very well, thank you. Witness, have you managed to read these last two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: The El Jihad group is mentioned here. What was your information about that group?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The fact itself that they were referred to by different names, Jihad, Mujahid, Mujahedin, indicates we didn't even know their real name, never mind any other details about their structure. But the problem that we are talking about here is the fact that they attracted a large number of people which were from the -- from our unit, and also they attracted a large number of persons who had not been mobilized into the 306th Mountain Brigade yet. People were going to different units while at the time we were at an elevation of over 1800 meters, and we had to hold an enormous line for which task we did not have enough men or weapons or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to -- to ask you this now: You, as the author of this document, sent the document to the 3rd Corps. Did you ever receive confirmation from the 3rd Corps that any unit named "El Jihad" was established?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the usher to put away this document and to show the witness Exhibit 145, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to draw your attention to the first part of this official note of the 306th Brigade, dated the 26th of August, 1993. Can you please look at the first half of the document, where the situation in Guca Gora is being described, the burning of buildings belonging to Croats. It also says that the perpetrators are foreign nationals who are currently living in "our area of responsibility." Please, is this the situation that you were just describing when you were talking about burning?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was something that was repeated several times. This was not the only such instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the following: Did you find out, you and the brigade, did you find out who were the perpetrators of this incident that is described in this document?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's this group called "Abu Hamza's group." The only thing we knew was that they were living in Guca Gora. As for any other details, how many of them were there and so on, we didn't know that and it was something that we couldn't really find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, you mentioned in your testimony the group from Mehurici and this group from Guca Gora, and my question to you is this: Did these groups take part, together with you -- when I say "with you," I'm thinking of the 306th Brigade. Did they take part in combat actions together with the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, none of these groups ever participated in combat actions together with us, nor was it possible to establish any kind of contact or cooperation. You could say more, that we were kind of hostile towards each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we put this document away now. I would like the witness to look at Exhibit number 263. For the transcript, this is a document of the 306th Brigade of the 28th of July, 1993, and its title is "Information on the Situation and factors of influence on combat morale in the area of responsibility and units of the 306th Mountain Brigade." I would like the witness to look at page 3 of the Bosnian version, which is page 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you look at the signature part of the page?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This is my handwriting, my signature. This is a document that I thus drafted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you please look at -- you are the author of the document, so, first of all, can you please, but just briefly, explain the context in which this document was written?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Because of the facts that I described earlier, that in our area of responsibility there was a large number of refugees, a large number of different armed groups about which we had no information who they were, what they were, where they were from, and we were unable to identify them in any way, and we wished to have the situation under control as much as we could. In this document, we resolved a large number of problems that we were facing as a unit, and generally as the local population, because most of our fighters came from that area. So anything that was happening in that area had an adverse effect on the combat morale, so this is what I was specifically informing about in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I would like you to look at the beginning of the document, the part -- well, actually, can you scroll the document down. You already explained that maybe we can scroll down this document. Can you please -- I'm interested in this part here at Hrasce. It begins somewhere towards the end of the document, it says: "At Hrasce," and then "(688)." This is page 2 of the English version. Can the usher please show us page 2 of the English version, the third paragraph from the bottom. Page 2, the third paragraph from the bottom. Okay, we can see it. Thank you. What is described here are some activities that relate to the Hrasce feature. The units that tried to capture it are mentioned. I'm going to quote: "In Hrasce (688), where the latest offensive conducted by our forces failed, and the 17th, the 314th, the Mujahedin and our forces tried the same several times, but it was unsuccessful just like it was this time." I would like you to comment on this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This time, the 306th Mountain Brigade tried to capture feature 688 called "Hrasce." We were not successful. We had many losses, because of which our failure prompted different not-so-nice tales to circulate in the brigade, and I mentioned the units which had earlier, on several occasions, each on its own, attempted to eliminate this feature, because it was in a dominant position in the middle of the Bila Valley, and it was possible to control all the roads from there, all the roads that lead through the Bila Valley. So this was something that was in the way of the 17th Glorious, which had to effect the replacements of its fighters through our area of responsibility, and it was an obstacle to the 314th as well, which had to also relieve its own troops by passing through our area of responsibility, as well as an obstacle to the Mujahedin, who particularly did not allow movement, as well as members of the 306th Mountain Brigade, who whenever they wanted to were not able to carry out their regular activities. And numbering the -- or mentioning the units here, I would put a comma after that, and I put "our forces" too, but that does not mean that we ever took part together with any of these units in attempts to eliminate this feature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago, you said that you had never -- that you had never fought together, side by side, with a Mujahedin, in no action. Did you ever fight together with them, and I mean the 306th, in any action connected with the -- in relation to elevation Hrasce?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may remove this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before it gets removed and then I get confused, Madam Vidovic, because this document, which is authored by this witness, says: "In Hrasce (688), where the latest offensive conducted by our forces failed, 17th, 314th, Mujahedin and our forces tried the same several times, but it was unsuccessful like this time." Now, that, together with what he has just said a few minutes ago before you asked the question, he said, at page 40, it's a very long sentence: "So this was something that was in the way of the --" Sorry, page 40, line 5: "So this was something that was in the way of 17th Glorious, which had to effect the replacements of its fighters through our area of responsibility, and it was an obstacle to the 314th as well, which had to," I don't know what, "its own troops by passing through the area of responsibility, as well as an obstacle to the Mujahedin, who particularly did not allow movement, as well as members of the 306th Mountain Brigade, who, whenever they wanted to, were not able to carry out their regular activities." So it looks like all four, the 17th Glorious, the 314th, the Mujahedin and the 306th Mountain Brigade had similar obstacles which they were together facing, which tends to corroborate what is said in this document, but which is contradictory to what I hear the witness saying. Are you able to explain this, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This sentence is rather long, and especially now, listening to the translation, I myself find it difficult to understand what you are saying, because it does not exactly correspond to what it was that I meant to say, initially. What it is is that this feature, Hrasce feature, is in a dominant position in the central part of the Bila Valley. Many units that had to pass that way were stopped, and each of them separately, when they were threatened from this feature, they tried to eliminate the weapons or the army -- members of the army that were up there. So it was never any of these units together. They all acted separately. Whenever they were prevented to move on and proceed along the route, they would try to eliminate them, but they never tried to do it together, all of them together, they did it separately, each on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you then explain the contents of your letter, of your report, sir, which says, I repeat: "In Hrasce, (688), where "The latest offensive conducted by our forces failed, 17th, 314th, Mujahedin and our forces tried the same several times, but it was unsuccessful like this time." This is what you wrote, or at least the English translation of what is alleged to have been written by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was the assistant commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade, and when I say "our forces" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just explain that sentence that I have just talked about. You have told us that you were the assistant commander. Don't start there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it says here that earlier on -- just a moment, please: "Earlier on, the following units tried or attempted to capture this feature."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading from, sir, in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my document, there is a sentence reading as follows: "At Hrasce (688), where the latest offensive mounted by our forces failed," and I'm referring here to the 306th, earlier on at this feature, the 17th, the 314th, the Mujahedin and "our forces also attempted," in other words, also our brigade, the 306th Brigade at some point in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the English version, there's no --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I was saying in the English, there is no phrase "earlier on," but nonetheless, you still trap together the 17th, the 314th, the Mujahedin, and "our forces" having tried the same several times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Each of these units had attempted this earlier on, and so did the 306th on one occasion before this one that I was now reporting on. So this was our second failure, and all of these units had attempted to eliminate this feature, but none of them was successful. And yet we were the only ones who were proclaimed uncapable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand, though, that the reader of this sentence, without the use of the words that all of these units attended independently and separately, would understand this sentence to mean that they actually did attempt -- took this attempt together. This is the problem, you see. Your document doesn't say you did this independently and separately. It just lists the people -- the groups that did it and leaves the reader with the impression that you were in a joint action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible to read this document in that light, but these words that I mentioned here "earlier on," these units, and then I named all the units, also tried their hand at this. It doesn't mean that they all did this together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even if you put the words "earlier on," it still gives the same impression, without using words "independently" or "separately" or something to that effect. It just says: "Earlier on, the 17th, 314th, Mujahedin and our forces tried the same several times ..." That is what it says, and that is what the reader is left with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the possible interpretation of this, but the sentence is a bit long and unwieldy, but it does reflect what I mentioned here. At least that's how I attempted to report it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you a question relating to this. In this period, in the summer of 1993, did the units mentioned here, the 17th, the 314th, the Mujahedin and the 306th, ever together attack the Hrasce feature?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, never, not the four together nor either of these units in combination with one other unit. All of them just attempted this separately much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If this is the fact -- sorry. If this is the fact, Mrs. Vidovic, the question that springs to mind is: Why not? Why was an attempt never made to coordinate the forces and to take this hill in a joint and coordinated action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because all our forces, in fact, still had their own priorities, tasks, that related to the defence of the defence line facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, and only in those cases, where we were stopped by forces and where parts of our forces were prevented to move further, only on those occasions did we attempt to eliminate this feature. In other words, we did not have time to deal with this feature, in view of far greater problems that we faced at the time on the defence line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, just organize the operations in a separate fashion. You had to coordinate your action at one point in time, or didn't you have to do that? Otherwise, you could have -- you could have ended up on the elevation, all of you at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. All these units, from time to time every one of these units would pass through that area, and on those occasions where they were stopped from progressing further, they would then draw attempt -- they would then enter into conflict with those who were on this feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was not -- the taking of this elevation was not a coordinated action, but the point was just to be able to go through this area when needed; that was the whole idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because from this feature, it was possible to control all movement through the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it's because I'm a woman, but I'm having a hard time with this. I'm sorry. But if taking this elevation was really necessary to control passage, taking this elevation in order to control it must have been an operation that would have been decided and coordinated by the superior command of the units that were going through. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you, but units have their priorities, and this feature, although it was just a single, tiny feature, it was very well fortified and we were not able to mount a large operation for just this one point that would occasionally prevent movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm getting even more confused, the more I hear you. You told us that you never undertook a joint effort to take this feature because your forces still had their own priorities related to the defence of the defence line facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. But in the same breath, you say this was an important feature that controlled movement. And, in fact, to underline how important it is, there have been four separate units that have attempted to take this feature, and all of them have failed. Yours, in particular, has tried it twice and has twice failed. Surely, this is an important priority, it looks like, that needs to be taken in order to control movement. And the question that the Judge raised then remains unanswered, "Why was there no joint effort mounted to take this important feature that controls movement which has been attempted by four separate units who have failed?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to answer this question, why we did not communicate more together. I think what was at stake here was the interests of each separate unit, and they're focusing on their own tasks, so it wasn't really perceived as a joint problem to such an extent that we would actually sacrifice a large number of people for just this one feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me ask you what, I hope, will be my last question on this point. All these four units that attempted to take this feature had a common goal and a common objective about this feature, and they were -- although they attended to take the feature at different times and independently of one another, they were both -- they were all interested in freeing this feature for their common purpose; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
